summary: exec: Cleanup POSIX timers right after de_thread()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

exec: Cleanup POSIX timers right after de_thread()

A per-thread CPU timer holds a reference to the PID of the thread it is
attached to and, while it is armed, its node is queued in that thread's
posix_cputimers. The task is looked up by that PID.

When a non-leader thread exec()s, de_thread() changes which task owns
that PID. pid_task(timer->it.cpu.pid, PIDTYPE_PID) then returns NULL,
but the node is still queued on tsk, which is alive. timer_lock_sighand()
takes a failed lookup to mean that the node is already dequeued, so it
has nothing to undo.

begin_new_exec() calls posix_cpu_timers_exit(me) right after
exec_task_namespaces() and that removes the leftover node, so the state
normally stays invisible. But bprm->point_of_no_return is set before
de_thread(), so if unshare_files(), set_mm_exe_file(), exec_mmap() or
exec_task_namespaces() fails, the task dies before it gets there.
exit_itimers() then frees the k_itimer while its node is still queued,
and reaping tsk later erases that freed node from the rbtree.

In short:

      the non-leader thread B           the parent

  timer_create(CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID)
  timer_settime()
    arm_timer()            // the node is queued on B
  execve()
    de_thread(B)
      exchange_tids(B, leader)  // B's PID now belongs to the leader
      release_task(leader)
        __exit_signal(leader)
          posix_cpu_timers_exit(leader)  // cleans leader's queue, not B's
          __unhash_process(leader)  // that PID has no task anymore
    exec_mmap()
      mmap_read_lock_killable(old_mm)
                                kill(B, SIGKILL)
      // -EINTR
  get_signal()
    do_exit()
      exit_itimers()
        posix_timer_delete()
          posix_cpu_timer_del()
        posix_timer_unhash_and_free()  // freed while still queued
                                wait4()
                                  release_task(B)
                                    posix_cpu_timers_exit(B)
                                      cleanup_timerqueue()
                                        timerqueue_del()  // use-after-free

Move the POSIX timer cleanup right after de_thread() before any of the
later failure conditions brings the task into do_exit().

[ tglx: Move the cleanup right after de_thread() ]

summary: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum

If a packet with bad checksum metadata gets into the ipv4 stack,
skb_checksum_help can corrupt the network header and cause a bunch of
mischief.

This was discovered and reported by Paulos, and has been reporoduced
by others independently since.

We really shouldn't allow such packets in, but as a defence
in depth measure, let's also check before we complete the checksum.

A more complete validation at input is forthcoming, but needs more work.

summary: KVM: x86/mmu: Cap number of parent PTEs per SP at 1000 (the arbitrary rmap limit)
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86/mmu: Cap number of parent PTEs per SP at 1000 (the arbitrary rmap limit)

When potentially reusing a shadow page, zap the shadow page if its number
of parent PTEs exceeds KVM's (mostly) arbitrary rmap recycling threshold.
Letting the guest create a (mostly) unbounded number of parent PTEs allows
the guest to coerce KVM into creating lists containing millions of PTEs,
effectively bounded only by the maximum number of shadow pages.

Because PTE lists are simple singly linked lists, removal is O(n).  Even
worse, if a list is constructed just so, teardown can be O(n^2), e.g. if
SPTEs are built such that zapping child SPTEs always zaps the last entry
in the list.  To cap things off, all paths that walk PTE lists do so
while holding mmu_lock, without conditionally rescheduling.

Using a doubly linked list would not address the issue, as removal would
remain O(n) since KVM still wouldn't know where in the list to remove from.
Removal could be made O(1) by storing a per-SPTE pointer, but that would
largely defeat the purpose of reusing SPs, and would penalize well-behaved
guests, especially for nested TDP where aliasing page tables is uncommon.

So, cap the maximum number of parent PTEs at the rmap limit.  In practice,
well-behaved guests will likely never run afoul of the limit.  E.g. when
running Linux as L1 with TDP, the number of parent PTEs for a single SP
tops out at under 200 (though undoubtedly obscure workloads can push it
higher).  Deliberately use a "greater than or equal" as opposed to rmap's
strictly "greater than", as the rmap code checks the threshold immediately
*after* inserting into the list, i.e. the limit is 1000 for rmaps, KVM just
very briefly blows past it.

Apply the check to both indirect and direct SPs, because while a fully
direct MMU naturally limits the number of parent PTEs to '1', direct SPs in
indirect MMUs have no such constraint.  E.g. if the guest maps a huge PTE
into many locations in its page tables, and KVM is backing the hugepage
with a direct SP, i.e. with a series of smaller pages, then KVM could end
up with a direct SP with many parents.

Note, shadow_mmu_try_split_huge_pages() always restarts the rmap walk or
bails entirely if it gets to the point where it tries to grab a SP, i.e.
there is *no* pre-existing bug that would be tripped by zapping a SP and
thus rmaps when getting a SP.

summary: Bluetooth: L2CAP: Only accept connection responses to outstanding requests
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: L2CAP: Only accept connection responses to outstanding requests

An outgoing channel waits in BT_CONNECT until security
and the feature mask exchange complete, and only then
sends its connection request. A peer can answer it
before that with a connection response matching our
source CID. The channel then moves to BT_CONFIG,
completes configuration and becomes connected before
security has completed. If security then fails,
l2cap_security_cfm() leaves the connected channel
alone, so it stays up on a link that did not reach
the required security level.

A connection response with a zero source CID is
matched by identifier. Another channel can hold the
same identifier for a response it still has to send,
so the lookup can pick the wrong channel.

Only accept a connection response while our request
is outstanding, and only look at such channels when
matching by identifier.

summary: io_uring: free the task context after a grace period
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring: free the task context after a grace period

A task other than the owner can free a request, io_ring_exit_work()
running the local task_work of a DEFER_TASKRUN ring for example, or
io_do_iopoll() reaping completions. io_put_task() then takes the else
branch:

    percpu_counter_sub(&tctx->inflight, 1);
    if (unlikely(atomic_read(&tctx->in_cancel)))
            wake_up(&tctx->wait);
    put_task_struct(tctx->task);

The first line is what lets the owner leave io_uring_cancel_generic(),
and on exec it frees the tctx right after. Nothing holds that off for
the remaining three lines, the task reference only covers a tctx freed
along with the task_struct. It used to work out because
io_uring_del_tctx_node() took the uring_lock that the freeing side holds
across io_put_task(), until that moved to tctx_lock.

Free the tctx with kfree_rcu(), and enter an RCU read section in
io_put_task() before the count is dropped.

summary: mm/mglru: don't use stack pointers when walking PUD and PMD tables
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/mglru: don't use stack pointers when walking PUD and PMD tables

MGLRU passes stack copies of page-table entries in walk_pud_range() and
walk_pmd_range() when walking to the next level. These copies can become
stale when khugepaged or MADV_DONTNEED (CONFIG_PT_RECLAIM) removes a PTE
table concurrently.

This pattern dates back to commit bd74fdaea146 ("mm: multi-gen LRU:
support page table walks"). Likely, earlier locking masked the latent
bug. Later changes exposed it: commit 1d65b771bc08 ("mm/khugepaged:
retract_page_tables() without mmap or vma lock") allowed concurrent
retraction, and commit cf4a65539c13 ("memcg-v1: no need for memcg locking
for MGLRU") dropped the walker's outer RCU protection.

The fix is simple, so just fix the original commit so we don't have to
speculate. To fix it, pass the actual PMD/PUD pointers. This restores the
RCU-protected lookup and validation against the live PMD. Note that the PUD
handling is required as well to handle folded page tables correctly in all
cases.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private.

[ david: handle walk_pud_range() as well, clarify+simplify description,
         adjust Fixes: ]

summary: net: atl1c: drop oversized RX frames instead of panicking
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: atl1c: drop oversized RX frames instead of panicking

atl1c sizes its receive buffers from the netdev MTU plus a fixed set of L2
overheads, which comes to 1522 bytes at the default MTU.  A link partner
that sends a longer frame - in practice a MikroTik CCR2004-1G-2XS-PCIe,
whose RouterOS side defaults to l2mtu 1600 while the host stays at MTU 1500
- makes the length reported by the RX return descriptor exceed what the
hardware wrote, and skb_put() then either includes bytes that were never
received or trips skb_over_panic and takes the host down.

Compare the descriptor length against buffer_info->length, the length the
hardware was given, rather than against skb_tailroom(): the skb carries 64
bytes of slack for the DMA erratum, so tailroom is larger than the DMA
buffer and a frame in between would pass the check and still be delivered
with a tail the device never wrote.  The same test rejects frames shorter
than ETH_HLEN + ETH_FCS_LEN; before this change a reported length below
ETH_FCS_LEN underflowed in skb_put().

The frame is dropped with kfree_skb_reason(SKB_DROP_REASON_PKT_TOO_BIG) so
drop_monitor and the kfree_skb tracepoint see it, and counted through
dev_core_stats_rx_dropped_inc(), which survives atl1c_get_stats()
overwriting the hardware counters on every read.  It also counts as work:
atl1c_clean_rfd() has already recycled the RFD, and the refill at the end
of the poll only runs when work_done is non-zero, so sustained oversized
traffic would otherwise drain the ring and stop RX.

Tested on a MikroTik CCR2004-1G-2XS-PCIe (4x AR8151) in a Proxmox VE host,
with atl1c built from a DKMS tree carrying this change: the l2mtu-1600
traffic that panics the stock driver is dropped and counted with the patch
applied, and received normally once the host MTU is raised to match.

This complements commit 36c2009d90f2 ("net: atl1c: fix soft lockup on
out-of-range tpd_cons read"), which fixed the TX side of the same
"host dies while the card resets" problem.

summary: batman-adv: tt: ignore ROAM flag of received ADD changes
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: tt: ignore ROAM flag of received ADD changes

A received TT change (OGM diff or full table response) with the ROAM flag
but without DEL is handled by batadv_tt_global_add() like a ROAMING_ADV:

* a newly created global entry gets BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM and is
  therefore excluded from the global CRC. The sender has it in its local
  CRC and the receiver has to request the full table again
* batadv_tt_global_purge_local() removes the local entry of the
  receiver. The receiver's own client is considered as roamed to the sender
  and frames for it are rerouted

The ROAM flag only has a meaning together with DEL. Drop it on reception to
keep it from populating the global table with a temporary ROAMING entry
which is not part of the CRC - and therefore causing a CRC mismatch.

summary: drm/drm_crtc: ensure dma_fence_ops remain valid during device unbind
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/drm_crtc: ensure dma_fence_ops remain valid during device unbind

In [1], sashiko reported the following issue:

=== snip ===
Looking at how these fences are managed, drm_crtc_create_fence()
creates a dma_fence without taking a reference to the drm_device or
drm_crtc. Because the sync_file framework exposes this fence to
userspace, the fence can outlive the CRTC.

The dma_fence contract requires that data accessed by dma_fence_ops
(like get_driver_name) must remain valid for an RCU grace period after
the fence is signaled. However, drm_crtc_cleanup() and the subsequent
freeing of the device do not wait for an RCU grace period via
synchronize_rcu().

If userspace calls ioctl(SYNC_IOC_FILE_INFO) concurrently with a device
hot-unplug:

CPU1 (Userspace)
sync_file_get_name()
  ops = rcu_dereference(fence->ops);
  if (!dma_fence_test_signaled_flag())
    // Preempted or delayed here

CPU2 (Driver Teardown)
Signals the fence (setting fence->ops = NULL)
Destroys and frees the CRTC without waiting for an RCU grace period

CPU1 (Resumes)
  ops->get_driver_name(fence) -> drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name()
  crtc = fence_to_crtc(fence); // Casts to the freed CRTC
  return crtc->dev->driver->name; // Use-after-free

...

Does the CRTC or DRM device need to be kept alive for the RCU grace
period, or should the fence hold a proper reference to prevent the
use-after-free when get_driver_name() and get_timeline_name() access
the freed CRTC structure?
=== snap ===

I believe this to be a correct observation and this patch implements
the suggestion of waiting for an RCU grace period before proceeding
with destruction of the drm_crtc, so that get_driver_name() and
get_timeline_name() can still work.

summary: nvme-rdma: fix NULL queue->ctrl dereference on reconnect
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvme-rdma: fix NULL queue->ctrl dereference on reconnect

Since commit 2a8513091d2f ("nvme-rdma: parallelize I/O queue allocation
and startup"), a reconnect that gets more I/O queues than before grows
the tag set before the new queues are set up. queue->ctrl is only set
by nvme_rdma_setup_io_queues(), so I/O submitted in between reaches
nvme_rdma_queue_rq() on a queue that was never allocated and
dereferences a NULL queue->ctrl:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 000000000000034c
  RIP: 0010:nvme_rdma_queue_rq+0x52/0xb90

Set queue->ctrl for every queue when allocating the controller. Such
requests are then requeued like on any other queue that is not live.

summary: scsi: target: Verify the iSCSI ISID is null-terminated
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: target: Verify the iSCSI ISID is null-terminated

iscsi_parse_pr_out_transport_id() returns the ISID of a FORMAT CODE 01b
TransportID as a pointer into the PERSISTENT RESERVE OUT parameter list,
lowercased in place and never null-terminated.  spc4r37 Table 508 requires
the field to be null-terminated, but a non-conforming initiator can omit
the NULL; when the ISID ends at the end of the received buffer, the pointer
is not a C string.

The registration code still consumes it as one: strcmp() in
__core_scsi3_locate_pr_reg() and in the REGISTER AND MOVE path, and
snprintf("%s") in __core_scsi3_do_alloc_registration(), which also reads
its first 8 bytes unconditionally with get_unaligned_be64() - a NUL check
does not bound that read.

When the parameter list spans more than one page, transport_kmap_data_sg()
maps it with vmap(), and the over-read walks off the end of the mapping
into the vmalloc() guard page and oopses.  Reproduced with a PR OUT
REGISTER + SPEC_I_PT parameter list of exactly 8192 bytes whose final
TransportID carries a 12-byte ISID without a terminating NUL:

  BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffc9000138c000
  RIP: 0010:strcmp+0xc/0x30
  Call Trace:
   __core_scsi3_locate_pr_reg+0xd3/0x120 [target_core_mod]
   core_scsi3_decode_spec_i_port+0x8fc/0x13a0 [target_core_mod]
   core_scsi3_emulate_pro_register+0x73c/0x900 [target_core_mod]
   ...
   iscsi_target_rx_thread+0xef/0x1d0 [iscsi_target_mod]

With a single-page parameter list the buffer is a kmap() direct mapping, so
the over-read continues into the physically adjacent page instead of
faulting.  snprintf("%s") then copies whatever follows the ISID in memory
into pr_reg_isid, and PR IN READ FULL STATUS reports the registration back
to any initiator, turning the over-read into an info leak of kernel heap
contents.  Reproduced with a 4096-byte parameter list whose last
TransportID ends at the end of the buffer with a 4-byte ISID and no NUL,
interleaved with I/O to populate adjacent pages: the READ FULL STATUS
response returned the ISID as "0xleak" followed by raw bytes that were not
part of the parameter list.  The snprintf() into
pr_reg_isid[PR_REG_ISID_LEN] caps the echoed ISID at 15 characters, so at
most 11 bytes past the buffer are leaked per command, but the PR OUT
command is not rate limited.

Any initiator that can send PR OUT to an iSCSI-exported LUN can trigger
either variant, including a guest via vhost-scsi.

Require 8 bytes to remain after the ",i,0x" separator, and a NUL inside the
rest of the descriptor, before the ISID pointer is returned.  REGISTER AND
MOVE fails with TCM_INVALID_PARAMETER_LIST; on SPEC_I_PT no target port
claims the malformed TransportID, and the command fails the same way.

summary: 9p/trans_virtio: reject mount tags longer than NAME_MAX at probe
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

9p/trans_virtio: reject mount tags longer than NAME_MAX at probe

p9_virtio_probe() reads a 16-bit mount tag length (tag_len) from the
device config and kzalloc()s tag_len + 1 bytes for chan->tag with no
upper bound. A malicious or compromised host can present a tag of up to
65535 bytes; that tag is later copied into the single-page sysfs buffer
by p9_mount_tag_show() (memcpy(buf, chan->tag, tag_len + 1)), a
host-controlled out-of-bounds write of up to ~64 KiB past the PAGE_SIZE
attribute buffer.

Reject an overlong tag at probe time. A 9p mount tag is a name-like
identifier, so bound it by NAME_MAX (255): that limit is independent of
the sysfs/seq_file page size and is far above any legitimate mount tag,
which keeps p9_mount_tag_show() safe at the root without hard-coding a
seq_file implementation detail.

summary: io_uring: defer foreign io-wq enqueues to task_work
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring: defer foreign io-wq enqueues to task_work

An IOPOLL ring without DEFER_TASKRUN can be reaped by a task other than
the one that submitted the I/O. If a polled request is marked
REQ_F_REISSUE, io_free_batch_list() calls io_queue_iowq() with the
original tctx. Ordinary task exit can tear down tctx->io_wq after
draining only the tracked requests. The live request pins the task, but
not its io-wq, so the foreign task can race io_wq_put_and_exit() and
enqueue through a freed or NULL queue.

Forward foreign userspace enqueues to the owning task before accessing
tctx->io_wq. Use a dedicated task_work callback so reissues still go
straight to io-wq, and fail them if task_work is running in cancellation
mode. Preserve the existing PF_KTHREAD cancellation path. This also
covers the other callers of io_queue_iowq() without changing the
worker-owned enqueue path.

summary: iommu/amd: Force device table to maximum size
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommu/amd: Force device table to maximum size

IOMMU can perform out-of-bounds read of the device table entry (DTE)
that is adjacent to the last DTE and falls outside the device table.
For example, if the device table can hold 0 to N-1 entries, then the
IOMMU can be made to fetch the Nth entry, which falls outside the
device table.

The device table is owned by the hypervisor (HV) and is assigned in 4KB
pages that are contiguous in system physical address (SPA). If the
out-of-bound DTE falls on a guest-owned page, then the guest can exploit
this bug to setup malicious table walks to corrupt HV pages and/or bring
down the system. Note that this bug does not manifest when the device
table size is set to its maximum size of 2MB.

Therefore, force the device table size to the maximum 2MB on affected
processors. These are CPU family 0x17 (Zen1/Zen2) through family 0x1a
(Zen5/BRH).

This is a mitigation for CVE-2024-21963.

kdump reuses the previous kernel's device table only when the size
encoded in the IOMMU device-table register matches
pci_seg->dev_table_size. A mixed rollout disagrees: the unpatched
kernel uses the IVRS-derived size and the patched kernel uses 2MB,
so __reuse_device_table() rejects the table. On SNP-capable IOMMUs
that rejection panics the kdump kernel. Kernels that both have this
patch agree on 2MB and reuse succeeds. Update the production kernel
and the crash kernel together.

summary: Bluetooth: L2CAP: Reject signalling responses in invalid states
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: L2CAP: Reject signalling responses in invalid states

A peer can send configuration messages while an
incoming channel is in BT_CONNECT2, before the
security or deferred accept gate has completed. A
configuration response can then promote the channel
to BT_CONNECTED. Configuration responses can also
act on channels that are closing, and a late connection
response can move a disconnecting channel back to
BT_CONFIG.

Accept connection responses only while waiting in
BT_CONNECT. Answer configuration requests in
BT_CONNECT2, but defer our own request until
BT_CONFIG so configuration cannot complete before
the gate. Ignore configuration responses outside
BT_CONFIG and BT_CONNECTED, and only complete
configuration in BT_CONFIG.

summary: io_uring/io-wq: save worker type before dropping its reference
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/io-wq: save worker type before dropping its reference

io_wq_cancel_tw_create() inspects cb->func after calling
io_worker_cancel_cb(). For an existing worker, that call can drop the
last worker reference and wake io_worker_exit(). If the canceling task
is preempted, the worker can be unlinked and freed by kfree_rcu() before
the callback function is inspected. KASAN reports a slab-use-after-free
read in this path.

Save whether the callback belongs to an unpublished continuation worker
while its reference is still held, then use the saved result for the
conditional free. This preserves the existing accounting and frees only
the worker allocated for the canceled continuation.

summary: drm/loongson: Fix double free on BO initialization failure
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/loongson: Fix double free on BO initialization failure

If ttm_bo_init_validate() fails, it drops the buffer object's reference
and cleans it up through the supplied destroy callback. lsdc_bo_destroy()
releases the GEM object and frees the enclosing lsdc_bo, so freeing it
again in lsdc_bo_create() causes a double free on a synchronous failure
path.

Let TTM own the cleanup after initialization has started and return the
error directly. Keep the explicit free on drm_gem_object_init() failure,
which occurs before ownership is passed to TTM.

Tested on LS7A2000 by making drm_vma_offset_add() return -ENOSPC for one
selected dumb-buffer creation. The error reached userspace, the destroy
callback ran once, and no handle was published or tracked BO retained.
Normal buffer creation, zeroing, mapping, readback and release passed.

AI assistance was used for the ownership analysis, fix, fault-injection
tools, build and test execution.

summary: smb/server: prevent file publication after tree disconnect
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb/server: prevent file publication after tree disconnect

TREE_DISCONNECT closes the tree's published file handles before marking and
removing the tree connection. A concurrent CREATE that already holds a tree
reference can therefore publish its file after the close pass. When CREATE
drops its reference, the tree can be freed while the published file still
points to it.

Mark and remove the tree connection before closing its files, and serialize
both new-open and durable-reconnect volatile ID publication with that state
transition. An opener is then either published in time for the close pass
or rejected after disconnect with STATUS_NETWORK_NAME_DELETED.

Keep a tree reference while a file carries its tree pointer. This protects
asynchronous users that can defer the file's final destruction past tree
disconnect.

The close pass can race the successful FP_NEW to FP_INITED transition.
Take the opening request's file reference atomically with that transition.
This keeps the file alive until request completion even if teardown removes
the ID immediately.

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in proc_show_files (fs/smb/server/vfs_cache.c:126)
  Read of size 4 at addr ff11000101540f80 by task poc/153

  Call Trace:
    proc_show_files (fs/smb/server/vfs_cache.c:126)
    seq_read_iter (fs/seq_file.c:231)
    proc_reg_read_iter (fs/proc/inode.c:299)
    vfs_read (fs/read_write.c:574)
    ksys_read (fs/read_write.c:716)
    do_syscall_64 (arch/x86/entry/syscall_64.c:84)
    entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe (arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S:121)

  Allocated by:
    ksmbd_tree_conn_connect (fs/smb/server/mgmt/tree_connect.c:35)
    smb2_tree_connect (fs/smb/server/smb2pdu.c:2819)
    handle_ksmbd_work (fs/smb/server/server.c:368)

  Freed by:
    kfree (mm/slub.c:6801)
    handle_ksmbd_work (fs/smb/server/server.c:332)

summary: batman-adv: stop originator purge worker before freeing TT
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: stop originator purge worker before freeing TT

batadv_mesh_free() releases the translation tables via batadv_tt_free()
before batadv_originator_free() stops orig_work. The purge worker can
therefore still run while the TT is torn down. When an originator times
out, batadv_purge_orig_ref() calls batadv_tt_global_del_orig(), which
loads tt.global_hash and walks all buckets while taking their locks:

  CPU0                          CPU1
  batadv_tt_free()              batadv_purge_orig()
                                  batadv_tt_global_del_orig()
                                    hash = ...tt.global_hash;
    batadv_tt_global_table_free()
      batadv_hash_destroy(hash);
                                    spin_lock_bh(&hash->list_locks[i]);

Disable orig_work at the beginning of batadv_mesh_free(), directly after
the mesh was marked as deactivating. The second
disable_delayed_work_sync() in batadv_originator_free() is harmless because
it is free'd anyway.

summary: cipso: fix optlen corruption in cipso_v4_delopt()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

cipso: fix optlen corruption in cipso_v4_delopt()

cipso_v4_delopt() recomputes the option length by walking the option
buffer after the CIPSO option has been moved out.  The walk then reads
the stale bytes at the tail of the buffer as option data, and a crafted
setsockopt(IP_OPTIONS) buffer can make it treat one of them as an option
length, increasing opt->opt.optlen beyond the valid option data.

The corrupted length stays on the socket and is later used as the copy
length by getsockopt(IP_OPTIONS) and by the udp/raw/ping sendmsg paths,
where it exceeds the size of the buffers they copy into.

Compute the new length from the intact options before the move and
subtract the CIPSO length, and fill the padding with IPOPT_END.

summary: sctp: account for chunk padding in sctp_init_cause()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: account for chunk padding in sctp_init_cause()

sctp_init_cause() accepts a chunk when skb_tailroom() can hold the
cause header and the payload. sctp_addto_chunk() then writes 0-3
bytes of padding before that header so the chunk stays 4-byte
aligned. The check does not include the padding, and the following
skb_put() calls skb_over_panic() from softirq.

Count the padding sctp_addto_chunk() is about to write. The cause
length on the wire stays the header plus the payload.

Found by LLM inspection, triggered and tested the fix.

summary: ASoC: SOF: Intel: hda-sdw-bpt: Stop active DMA before closing BPT streams
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ASoC: SOF: Intel: hda-sdw-bpt: Stop active DMA before closing BPT streams

When sdw_enable_stream() fails in intel_ace2x_bpt_send_async() after
hda_sdw_bpt_send_async() has already started the TX and RX DMA streams,
intel_ace2x_bpt_close_stream() invokes hda_sdw_bpt_close() directly
without calling hda_sdw_bpt_wait().  As a result,
hda_sdw_bpt_dma_deprepare() tears down the DMA buffers and BDL while
the DMA hardware is still running.

Disable any running TX or RX BPT DMA stream at the start of
hda_sdw_bpt_close() before unmapping channels and depreparing DMA
resources.

summary: mm/filemap: finish fault cleanup before dropping the fault lock
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/filemap: finish fault cleanup before dropping the fault lock

On a retried fault, a fatal signal interrupting the folio lock wait
makes lock_folio_maybe_drop_mmap() drop the fault lock without pinning
the file. However, filemap_fault() may still need to release
mapping->invalidate_lock. A concurrent munmap() can release the last
file reference and free the mapping before that unlock.

Defer dropping the fault lock to filemap_fault()'s retry cleanup, after
releasing invalidate_lock. If the fault lock was already dropped for
I/O, release the existing file reference instead. Keep the fault lock
held for FAULT_FLAG_RETRY_NOWAIT as before.

summary: ntfs: don't allow compression on volumes with clusters larger than 4K
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ntfs: don't allow compression on volumes with clusters larger than 4K

On a volume made with "mkntfs -c 8192", a user can set
FILE_ATTR_COMPRESSED on an empty file through system.ntfs_attrib.
Writing to the file and reading it back after dropping the page cache
then crashes:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in ntfs_read_compressed_block+0xa2c/0x2040
  Read of size 8192 at addr ffff88804355a000 by task dd/106

The read path only handles clusters up to 4K. It copies each cluster
out of a single page, and a compression block of 16 8K clusters does
not fit in the 64K ntfs_compression_buffer. Loading an inode already
rejects compressed data on such volumes.

Reject the flag change the same way.

summary: ocfs2: cache the mount context for dentry lock callbacks
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: cache the mount context for dentry lock callbacks

ocfs2_drop_dentry_lock() drops the inode reference before releasing the
DENTRY lock.  This lets inode eviction release the local inode and open
locks before a remote unlink can proceed past the DENTRY lock.

A DLM callback can still arrive before the DENTRY lock has been dropped.
ocfs2_get_dentry_osb() obtains the mount context through dl_inode->i_sb,
which can access a freed inode when the downconvert thread drops the
last inode reference in its post-unlock callback:

  Downconvert thread                     DLM callback thread
  ------------------                     -------------------
  ocfs2_process_blocked_lock()
    ocfs2_dentry_post_unlock()
      ocfs2_dentry_lock_put()
        ocfs2_drop_dentry_lock()
          iput(dl->dl_inode)
          [inode reclaimed after RCU]
                                         ocfs2_blocking_ast()
                                           ocfs2_get_dentry_osb()
                                             dl->dl_inode->i_sb
          ocfs2_simple_drop_lockres()

Store the mount context in the DENTRY lock resource's l_priv field and use
the default mount-context lookup.  Recover the containing dentry lock with
container_of(), as already done for refcount locks, and remove
ocfs2_get_dentry_osb().  ocfs2_dismount_volume() shuts down the DLM before
freeing the mount context, so callbacks can use it without accessing the
inode.  Preserve the existing iput-before-unlock order to avoid delaying
local inode and open lock release until after the DENTRY lock is released.

summary: xfs: mark the inode preallocated for pNFS write layouts past EOF
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: mark the inode preallocated for pNFS write layouts past EOF

xfs_fs_map_blocks() marks the inode XFS_DIFLAG_PREALLOC only when it
allocates blocks for a write layout. A write layout past EOF can also
hand out allocated blocks, such as speculative preallocation. blockgc
then frees them under the layout, and another file may get them.

Mark the inode whenever a write mapping ends past EOF.

summary: mm/huge_memory: fix list corruption when deferred_split_scan() races with deferred_split_folio()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/huge_memory: fix list corruption when deferred_split_scan() races with deferred_split_folio()

Since the deferred split queue became a list_lru, the isolate callback
moves the folios it took a reference on to an on-stack list, linked
through folio->_deferred_list, and deferred_split_scan() takes them off
that list with list_del_init() without holding the list_lru lock.

deferred_split_folio() does not know about the on-stack list. It only
holds the list_lru lock when it looks at the same list_head, and it can
run for such a folio: a THP is queued when it is mapped, as a candidate
for the underused check, and is queued "again" when a part of it gets
unmapped:

  CPU0 deferred_split_scan()          CPU1 deferred_split_folio()
  list_del_init(&folio->_deferred_list)
    next->prev = prev
    prev->next = next
    entry->next = entry
                                      list_lru_lock_irqsave()
                                      folio_set_partially_mapped()
                                      __list_lru_add()
                                        list_empty(item)  -> true
                                        list_add_tail(item, &l->list)
                                          item->next = &l->list
                                          item->prev = tail
    entry->prev = entry

The folio now sits on the list_lru with ->prev pointing to itself. The
next removal leaves the neighbours pointing to it, and they still do so
after the folio has been freed. With CONFIG_DEBUG_LIST:

  list_del corruption. prev->next should be ffd4000000270090, but was
  ffd4000000278090. (prev=ffd4000000270090)

Fix it by grabbing the lock around list_del_init() so
deferred_split_folio() cannot race with it.

summary: mm/khugepaged: flush deferred unmaps before dropping a failed folio
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/khugepaged: flush deferred unmaps before dropping a failed folio

collapse_file() can fail its reference-count or dirty-folio check after
unmapping with TTU_BATCH_FLUSH.  Both paths put back the isolated folio,
then unlock it and drop the lookup reference before reaching the common
try_to_unmap_flush().

The page-cache reference does not keep the folio stable once the lock is
released.  Another collapse can replace and free it.  With its PTEs
already gone, that collapse cannot flush the first task's per-task TLB
batch, and retract_page_tables() skips short or unaligned VMAs.  A CPU can
therefore retain a user translation to the freed folio.  This has been
reproduced with unprivileged MADV_COLLAPSE on a memfd.

Flush at out_unlock while the lookup reference and folio lock are still
held.  The common flush continues to cover the accumulated pagelist on
both success and rollback, preserving batching on successful collapses.

summary: net: restore refcount ordering for lockless socket access
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: restore refcount ordering for lockless socket access

Before commit fb041bb7c0a9 ("locking/refcount: Consolidate implementations
of refcount_t"), default builds implemented refcount_inc_not_zero() using
atomic_add_unless(), which provided full memory ordering on success. The
commit removed that ordering on weakly ordered architectures, allowing
accesses after a successful reference acquisition to be reordered before
it.

Use refcount_inc_not_zero_acquire() in the IPv4 and IPv6 established
lookups and in inet_twsk_purge(), where the socket is validated again
after taking a reference.

bpf_sk_assign() can receive a socket pointer obtained through BTF
without a reference. Use acquire ordering when it takes its own reference
for a refcounted socket.

Use refcount_set_release() when setting refcounts in the SYN cookie,
TCP Fast Open, request migration, and TIME_WAIT paths. Keep the existing
TIME_WAIT smp_wmb(), which separately orders the refcount store before
ehash publication.

summary: net/sched: sch_qfq: prevent aggregate self-replacement
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/sched: sch_qfq: prevent aggregate self-replacement

qfq_change_class() snapshots the current aggregate settings while
holding the qdisc tree lock, but drops the lock before selecting the
destination aggregate. During that gap, qfq_enqueue() can move the
class to an aggregate matching the requested settings.

When qfq_change_class() resumes, qfq_find_agg() then returns cl->agg.
If it is a singleton, qfq_deact_rm_from_agg() frees the aggregate
before qfq_add_to_agg() immediately accesses the same pointer, causing
a use-after-free.

While holding the tree lock, skip the replacement when the destination
is already the current aggregate. Any estimator replacement has already
completed, so the class change can finish normally.

summary: iommu/virtio: Reset device before deleting virtqueues on probe failure
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommu/virtio: Reset device before deleting virtqueues on probe failure

viommu_probe() marks the device DRIVER_OK before populating the event
virtqueue and registering the IOMMU device in sysfs.  viommu_fill_evtq()
hands the device a set of device-writable buffers through
virtqueue_add_inbuf(), so from that point on the device may write into
them and into the rings.

If either step fails, the error path deletes the virtqueues without
resetting the device first.  The event buffers are allocated with
devm_kmalloc_array() and are released as probe unwinds, so the device can
go on writing to memory that has been freed.

Reset the device before deleting the virtqueues, the way viommu_remove()
already does.

summary: srcu: Add list_splice_init_srcu()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

srcu: Add list_splice_init_srcu()

list_splice_init_rcu() makes a list look empty to new readers, waits for
the current ones with the given sync function, and only then links the
entries into the new list. The sync function takes no argument, so it
can wait for RCU readers but not for the readers of an srcu_struct.

Passing synchronize_rcu() for a list read under SRCU still builds, but
leaves SRCU readers on the entries while the last one's next pointer is
moved onto the new list head. nvme_remove_namespaces() does this today.

Add list_splice_init_srcu(), which waits for the readers of the given
srcu_struct instead.

summary: xfs: refuse a pNFS LAYOUTCOMMIT of a range without blocks
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: refuse a pNFS LAYOUTCOMMIT of a range without blocks

A client can commit a hole in a LAYOUTCOMMIT, because nfsd does not
check the extents against its layouts. xfs_iomap_write_unwritten() then
allocates written blocks there. A large hole overruns the block
reservation and shuts XFS down. A small one exposes stale data.

Refuse such a range with -EIO, using XFS_BMAPI_CONVERT_ONLY.

summary: vhost: fix used ring index wrap in vhost_add_used_n_in_order
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vhost: fix used ring index wrap in vhost_add_used_n_in_order

vhost_add_used_n_in_order() advances start by nheads[i] but wraps it
with a single subtraction.  If start + nheads[i] >= 2 * vq->num, start
can remain outside the ring.

With used-ring logging enabled, start > vq->num makes (vq->num - start)
underflow.  log_write() then sets bits beyond the dirty-log bitmap,
potentially corrupting adjacent userspace memory.  This is reachable on
the vhost-net TX path with VIRTIO_F_IN_ORDER: done_idx can reach
VHOST_NET_BATCH (64), triggering the issue with a 32-entry ring.

Wrap start with a mask to keep it within the ring.  VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM
enforces a nonzero power-of-two ring size, allowing start to be wrapped
using & (vq->num - 1).

summary: ceph: clamp the inline data length in ceph_fill_inline_data()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ceph: clamp the inline data length in ceph_fill_inline_data()

The MDS decides how much inline data to attach to a reply, and the
client parses inline_len without any upper bound: ceph_decode_need()
only verifies that the message actually carries that many bytes.
ceph_fill_inline_data() then copies the data into a single folio
with no length check, so a malicious or buggy MDS returning more
inline data than the folio can hold writes past its end.

Clamp the length to folio_size() so both callers, handle_cap_grant()
and fill_inode(), are covered.

summary: xfs: cap the block count of xfs_iomap_write_direct() at one extent
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: cap the block count of xfs_iomap_write_direct() at one extent

xfs_iomap_write_direct() reserves blocks for the whole count in an
unsigned int. For a pNFS layout the client chooses that count, and an
RW LAYOUTGET for 16 TiB wraps the reservation and shuts XFS down.

xfs_bmapi_write() maps at most XFS_MAX_BMBT_EXTLEN blocks here, so cap
the count at that. nfsd asks again for the rest. The other callers get
the same mapping as before.

summary: wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery

In AP mode every broadcast and multicast data frame is routed to
TX_DESC_QSEL_HIGH, the after-DTIM queue, whether or not anybody is
asleep. The firmware drains that queue at beacon pace, a dozen or so
frames per second measured on RTL8822BU, while one associated client's
mDNS/SSDP chatter alone exceeds that. The excess accumulates inside
the chip until the shared TX page pool is exhausted (measured: 14 of
1803 pages left). From that point every host-sourced frame queues
behind the backlog: authentication responses reach the air seconds
after the client has given up, so no station can associate anymore,
and the beacon reserved-page download fails the BCN_VALID poll
("error beacon valid") because it needs pages from the same pool. The
AP keeps beaconing, so the failure looks like a silent RX stall and
only a reboot recovers.

mac80211 already decides when after-DTIM delivery is needed: it sets
IEEE80211_TX_CTL_SEND_AFTER_DTIM on bmc frames only while at least one
station is actually dozing. Honor that instead of routing
unconditionally: flagged frames keep going through the high queue with
the MORE_DATA and HGQMD handling introduced by commit 076f786a0ae1
("wifi: rtw88: Fix AP mode incorrect DTIM behavior"), everything else
leaves at line rate through the AC queues. This partially reverts the
usb.c hunk of that commit, whose unconditional routing is what lets
the backlog build up.

On a bench AP (USB2, 20 MHz, WPA2, hostapd, a Windows client driven
through disconnect/reconnect cycles): reconnects fail 0/5 on RTL8822BU
and 0/3 on RTL8821CU before this change, and pass 10/10 and 5/5 with
it, with the page pool staying healthy and no beacon errors logged.

summary: can: protect the receive lists with a per-device lock
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

can: protect the receive lists with a per-device lock

The receive lists of a CAN device are located in the device's
can_ml_priv and travel with the device when it is moved to another
network namespace. But they are protected by the per-netns
rcvlists_lock. So can_rx_unregister() needs dev_net(dev) to pick the
right lock and silently returns when the passed namespace does not
match dev_net(dev) anymore.

isotp_release() and bcm_release() leave their notifier list before they
take any lock that serializes against the netdev notifier, which runs
under RTNL. When the bound device is moved to another namespace in this
window, the notifier skips the socket and the release path has to remove
the filters itself. isotp_release() passes the socket's namespace, which
does not match dev_net(dev) anymore. bcm_rx_unreg() passes dev_net(dev),
which can_rx_unregister() reads again for its check, so a namespace
change between both reads makes the check fail as well. In both cases
can_rx_unregister() silently returns. As can_rx_register() stores
rcv->sk without a reference, the remaining receivers point to the freed
socket (isotp) or the freed op (bcm):

  BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in isotp_rcv+0x1570/0x24d0
  Read of size 1 at addr ffff888118130552 by task isotp_ns_uaf/578
   can_rcv_filter+0x4af/0x8c0
   can_receive+0x28d/0x3c0
   can_rcv+0x2a9/0x310
   __netif_receive_skb_one_core+0x21a/0x260
   process_backlog+0x210/0x760

Besides this, the lists of a device are protected by the rcvlists_lock
of the namespace that is passed in. Callers which pass dev_net(dev) read
it at different times, so the same lists may be modified under the locks
of different namespaces while the device is moved.

Taking RTNL in these release paths is no option: raw_bind(),
raw_setsockopt() and raw_release() already hold RTNL while adding and
removing up to CAN_RAW_FILTER_MAX filters per socket, which unprivileged
users can trigger repeatedly and which makes RTNL a global bottleneck.

Instead fix the root cause and add a spinlock to struct
can_dev_rcv_lists, which protects the receive lists of a CAN device or
the 'any' CAN device lists of a namespace. It is initialized in
can_set_ml_priv(), which is used by all CAN network devices. With this,
can_rx_unregister() finds the subscription independently of the
current namespace of the device. The protocols keep the device valid
with their tracked references. The per-netns rcvlists_lock only protects
the receive list statistics anymore, and CAN_RAW, CAN_BCM and CAN_ISOTP
pass the namespace that has been used for can_rx_register().

So isotp_release() and bcm_release() now remove their filters correctly
without RTNL, and raw_release(), raw_setsockopt(), raw_bind() and
isotp_bind() do not need RTNL anymore and add and remove their filters
under lock_sock(). To serialize bind() with NETDEV_UNREGISTER, bind()
publishes the device inside the RCU section of its lookup, and
raw_notify() and isotp_notify() recheck the bound device under lock_sock().
As RTNL does not keep NETDEV_DOWN out of bind() anymore, bind() checks
IFF_UP after publishing the bound device, with a barrier pair against
raw_notify() and isotp_notify(), so a down transition during bind() is
still reported with ENETDOWN.

summary: mm/khugepaged: always recheck the pmd in try_collapse_pte_mapped_thp()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/khugepaged: always recheck the pmd in try_collapse_pte_mapped_thp()

try_collapse_pte_mapped_thp() drops the PTE lock after it has cleared the
page table, and takes the PMD lock and the PTE lock to remove it.

In between, MADV_DONTNEED with CONFIG_PT_RECLAIM can reclaim the
page table. The pmd_same() check is supposed to handle this, but it is
only done with CONFIG_SPLIT_PTE_PTLOCKS.

Fix it by performing the check unconditionally.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private.

[ david: adjust description ]

summary: mm/huge_memory: fix truncate racing with PMD zapping
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/huge_memory: fix truncate racing with PMD zapping

zap_huge_pmd_folio() removes the rmap before calling folio_mark_dirty().
If this was the last mapping, truncation can skip unmapping the folio
and proceed without waiting for the PMD lock, racing with dirtying.

ifs_set_range_dirty() can oops if MADV_DONTNEED races with
ftruncate() on XFS, when we get the folio set dirty after it was found
to not be mapped anymore.

Move folio_mark_dirty() and folio_mark_accessed() before rmap removal,
matching the PTE zap path. This keeps the folio mapped while updating
its state, so truncation must wait for the page table lock.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

[ david: simplify comment and description ]

summary: sctp: hold shkey across socket migration
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: hold shkey across socket migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers queued DATA skbs from the old socket to the
new one. skb_orphan() invokes sctp_wfree() during that transfer and drops
the skb-owned shared-key reference.

If userspace has removed that key from the association, this can be the
final reference. The following sctp_set_owner_w() then dereferences the
freed chunk->shkey while trying to take the new owner reference.

Take a temporary shared-key reference before orphaning the skb and release
it after the new owner has taken its reference. This preserves the selected
authentication key throughout the ownership transfer.

Bug found and triaged by OpenAI Security Research and
validated by Trail of Bits.

summary: drm/amd/display: Avoid closing unowned DDC pins
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amd/display: Avoid closing unowned DDC pins

[WHY]
dal_ddc_open() cleans up pins it acquires on later failures. If the
data-pin open fails, this attempt acquired nothing. If opening the
clock pin or configuring fails, dal_ddc_open() closes the pins it
opened. An extra dal_ddc_close() is unnecessary and unsafe:
GPIO_RESULT_ALREADY_OPENED can mean AUX owns the existing handles,
and closing them here would disrupt AUX.

[HOW]
Remove the extra dal_ddc_close() from the failed-open path.

(cherry picked from commit 175ae7772b68757b4932f34ff862923cab7abe21)

summary: mm: fix unmap_mapping_range() beyond 4 GiB on 32-bit
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm: fix unmap_mapping_range() beyond 4 GiB on 32-bit

Commit 9eab0421fa94 ("mm: fix unmap_mapping_range high bits shift bug")
made holebegin and holelen unsigned before they are shifted, by casting
them to pgoff_t. That is an unsigned long: on a 32-bit kernel the cast
cuts off the upper half of the two loff_t values, so a hole which begins
at 4 GiB or beyond is taken for one in the first 4 GiB of the file.

truncate_pagecache() passes the new size of the file and asks for private
COWed pages to be unmapped as well. If a file of 6 GiB is truncated to
5 GiB, everything from 1 GiB on is unmapped, and what a process has
written to a private mapping of the range between 1 GiB and 5 GiB is
lost: it reads the contents of the file again.

Where the range has an end, the wrong range is unmapped instead of the
right one. The page cache copes with that, as it unmaps every folio that
it removes. The callers which only have unmap_mapping_range() to get
rid of user mappings do not, for example drm_vma_node_unmap(), whose fake
offsets reach beyond 4 GiB on 32-bit, and revoke_iomem() with physical
addresses of more than 32 bits.

Cast to u64 instead. Nothing changes for 64-bit kernels.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private.

summary: mm/mmu_gather: fix flushing ranges with 4 GiB or larger
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/mmu_gather: fix flushing ranges with 4 GiB or larger

__tlb_adjust_range() takes the size of the range which has to be flushed
as an unsigned int. Its callers, tlb_flush_{pte,pmd,pud,p4d}_range(), get
and pass an unsigned long. Consequently, a range that is 4 GiB or larger
gets truncated, possibly to 0.

On arm64 with hugetlb, a 64k kernel can have 16 GiB hugetlb folios
mapped contiguously at the PMD level and flush them when unmapping, and a
16k kernel can flush 64 GiB PUDs through tlb_unshare_pmd_ptdesc(). So
at least these two scenarios are affected.

Fix it by flushing the proper range instead of the truncated one by
properly using "unsigned long" for range_size.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private.

[ david: use two-tab indent, simplify description ]

summary: udf: check the unallocated space table when it is loaded
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

udf: check the unallocated space table when it is loaded

udf_table_new_block() hands out the first block of the extent closest
to its goal and trusts that the extent covers at least one whole block
inside the partition.  Nothing checks that.  A zero-length extent makes
it return the block the extent points at, which need not be free, and
the subtraction of one block then underflows the length into the type
bits, turning the entry into a bogus continuation.  An extent running
past the end of the partition makes it return blocks behind the
partition.

Such tables are not only found on crafted images: until the previous
commit, udf_table_new_block() itself left zero-length extents behind
in tables written by mkudffs, and then converted them into extents
running past the partition.

Check every extent once when the table is loaded, and refuse
read-write access if one is empty, is not a whole number of blocks, or
does not lie inside the partition, in the same way as for other
allocation information the kernel cannot use.  Check first that the
table is an Unallocated Space Entry at all: the walk starts at the
offset of the allocation descriptors in one, and for a file entry that
offset lies before the inode's in-memory copy of the descriptors.
Treat a chain of allocation extent descriptors that leads back to
itself the same way: the walk would otherwise return the same extents
forever, and the mount would never finish.  Let a fatal signal
interrupt the walk and fail the mount.

Refusing read-write access to an empty extent is deliberate.  It shows
that an old kernel took the last block but left the entry behind.  If
consumed again, the entry returns an in-use block and turns into a huge
bogus extent.  Refusing the table before that
happens avoids this second allocation; the filesystem can still be
mounted read-only.  The check cannot detect every overlap that may
already exist in a damaged table.

This patch should be backported together with the previous one: that
patch stops creating new empty extents, and this one rejects existing
ones before they are consumed again.

summary: drm/amdgpu: keep the CS user fence BO in GTT
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu: keep the CS user fence BO in GTT

The CS ioctl hands the GPU the GART address of the user fence BO, but
since the BO keeps its own preferred and allowed domains, it no longer
makes sure the BO is in GTT. A user fence in a VRAM BO, which only needs
to be a page in size, gets its address from amdgpu_bo_gpu_offset(), which
warns about non-contiguous VRAM. On navi31, a CS with a user fence in a
4K VRAM BO, or in one created with AMDGPU_GEM_CREATE_VM_ALWAYS_VALID:

  WARNING: amdgpu_object.c:1531 at amdgpu_bo_gpu_offset+0x86/0xb0 [amdgpu], CPU#11: cs_gem_checks/18393
  RIP: 0010:amdgpu_bo_gpu_offset+0x86/0xb0 [amdgpu]
  Call Trace:
   <TASK>
   amdgpu_cs_parser_bos.isra.0+0x4eb/0x850 [amdgpu]
   amdgpu_cs_ioctl+0x97e/0x2510 [amdgpu]
   drm_ioctl_kernel+0xac/0x110 [drm]
   drm_ioctl+0x2c6/0x5b0 [drm]
   __x64_sys_ioctl+0xa0/0xf0
   do_syscall_64+0xa3/0x4d0
   entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x76/0x7e

and BOs which can't be in GTT at all, like GWS or OA ones of a page in
size, pass the checks as well.

Only take BOs which can't be anywhere else than in GTT as user fence,
which the CS then validates there along with its other BOs. While at it,
detect userptrs with amdgpu_ttm_tt_is_userptr(); amdgpu_ttm_tt_get_usermm()
returns NULL once the task which created the userptr is gone.

v2: only take BOs which can only be in GTT instead of special casing the
    user fence BO in the validation, use amdgpu_ttm_tt_is_userptr()
    (Christian)

(cherry picked from commit f16989def9561d04d0f2e77216f5319112d29bf1)

summary: smb: client: do not pass a NULL buf to is_oplock_break()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: do not pass a NULL buf to is_oplock_break()

receive_encrypted_read() sets *num_mids = 1 and never writes the
caller's bufs[]. Offload returns -1 with *num_mids = 0, so the
demultiplex thread skips the frame. The inline decrypt path
returns 0 even when smb2_find_mid() fails.

cifs_demultiplex_thread() then treats mids[i] == NULL as an
oplock break and calls is_oplock_break(bufs[i], server) with
bufs[i] still NULL. smb2_is_valid_oplock_break() reads
hdr.Command at offset 12 and oopses.

A large encrypted READ whose MessageId does not match is enough
to panic cifsd.

    Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address
    0xdffffc0000000001: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI
    KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range
    [0x0000000000000008-0x000000000000000f]
    CPU: 0 PID: 100 Comm: cifsd
    RIP: smb2_is_valid_oplock_break+0xc8/0x2270 [cifs]
    cifs_demultiplex_thread
    Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

Return -1 when inline decrypt finds no mid, and skip
is_oplock_break() plus the unknown-frame dump when bufs[i]
is NULL. receive_encrypted_standard() already assigns
bufs[*num_mids].

summary: SUNRPC: fix netns use-after-free in write_gssp()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

SUNRPC: fix netns use-after-free in write_gssp()

While fuzzing with a customized syzkaller, I hit a refcount warning in
xprt_alloc(), reached from a write to /proc/net/rpc/use-gss-proxy:

  refcount_t: addition on 0; use-after-free.
  WARNING: lib/refcount.c:25 at refcount_warn_saturate+0xf8/0x120
  CPU: 0 PID: 10404 Comm: syz.0.17 Not tainted 7.3.0-rc1-00096-gcfebfd3db73d
  Call Trace:
   <TASK>
   xprt_alloc+0x83f/0x9d0
   xs_setup_xprt+0xaf/0x3c0
   xs_setup_local+0x47/0x7f0
   xprt_create_transport+0x16c/0x730
   rpc_create+0x38e/0x7f0
   gssp_rpc_create+0xe2/0x180
   set_gssp_clnt+0xba/0x1b0
   write_gssp+0x200/0x310
   proc_reg_write+0x240/0x330
   vfs_write+0x2aa/0x1050
   ksys_write+0x12a/0x250
   do_syscall_64+0x117/0x750
   entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f
   </TASK>

create_use_gss_proxy_proc_entry() stores the struct net pointer as the
proc entry's private data without taking a reference on it, and an open
file descriptor does not pin the namespace either, as procfs only pins
the proc_dir_entry. write_gssp() reads that pointer back with
pde_data() and hands it to set_gssp_clnt(), which reaches xprt_init():

	xprt->xprt_net = get_net_track(net, &xprt->ns_tracker, GFP_KERNEL);

get_net_track() -> get_net() -> refcount_inc() is unconditional, so
rpc_create() assumes its caller holds a reference on args.net.
write_gssp() does not.

Dropping the last ns.count reference does not make the file go away.
__put_net() only queues cleanup_net() on a workqueue, and the
remove_proc_entry() that fences off further writes runs from the
rpcsec_gss pernet .exit method, that is, from inside cleanup_net(). A
write landing between those two points increments a refcount that is
already zero. cleanup_net() does not re-read ns.count, so the namespace
is freed anyway and the rpc_xprt -- along with the AF_LOCAL socket
opened for it -- is left pointing at freed memory. The resurrected
count is visible to the rest of that teardown too: with
CONFIG_IPV6_MROUTE the same cleanup_net() worker then trips
!mr_can_free_table() in ip6mr_free_table(), which tests check_net() on
the namespace it is freeing.

It reduces to opening /proc/net/rpc/use-gss-proxy inside a new network
namespace, calling setns() back to the original one to drop the last
reference, and then writing "1" to the still-open descriptor.

Take the reference in write_gssp() itself and refuse the write when the
namespace is already gone. This is what procfs does for every other
/proc/net file: get_proc_net() is maybe_get_net(PDE_NET(PDE(inode)))
and seq_open_net() returns -ENXIO when it fails. PDE_NET() cannot be
reused here because the parent directory /proc/net/rpc carries no
namespace pointer. Adding a .pre_exit to rpcsec_gss_net_ops so the
entry is removed earlier would only narrow the window, since pre_exit
also runs from cleanup_net().

Live namespaces are unaffected: a write still returns the error from
set_gssp_clnt(), a write of "2" still returns -EINVAL, and reads are
untouched.

summary: smb: smbdirect: don't wait for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: don't wait for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync()

smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync() waited for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED
after smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work() called rdma_disconnect(). That
can take very long, e.g. if the peer just disappeared, until the
rdma cm gives up, or forever if the event already happened, but the
status was overwritten afterwards.

This is not needed: smbdirect_socket_destroy() drains the qp under
rdma_lock_handler(), destroys it and calls rdma_destroy_id(), which
only waits for a currently running event handler and makes sure no
further events are delivered. The rest of the disconnect protocol
(DREQ/DREP and timewait for IB, abrupt close for iWarp) is handled
by the rdma core asynchronously. drivers/nvme/host/rdma.c also just
calls rdma_disconnect() and ib_drain_qp() before rdma_destroy_id().

So smbdirect_socket_destroy() now also accepts
SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTING and changes the status to
SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTED itself under rdma_lock_handler().

We could still get RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in the small
windows between rdma_unlock_handler() and rdma_destroy_id(),
but in that case smbdirect_connection_rdma_event_handler()
is basically a no-op.

summary: nvmet: don't return memory contents beyond valid data when reading ANA log page
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvmet: don't return memory contents beyond valid data when reading ANA log page

The host side does not know how much valid data will be returned by the target
so it will typically provide a buffer larger than the amount of valid data in
the ANA log page.  The memory allocation used by the target does not guarantee
that prior kernel memory contents will not be returned past the end of the valid
page data.  Fix this to ensure that the SGL is zeroed before copying the data.

summary: drm/amdgpu/userq: validate the moved individual BOs on restore
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu/userq: validate the moved individual BOs on restore

An individual BO of a user queue VM, i.e. one which doesn't share the
root reservation, goes to the individual needs_update list when it is
evicted. The user queue restore looked at vm->invalidated for them, which
the VM state machine rework turned into the always_valid evicted list and
commit 18decfc9e8cc ("drm/amdgpu/userq: actually validate userq BOs")
into the individual evicted one. That list only holds imported DMA-bufs of
compute VMs though, so for a user queue VM nothing is validated.

The restore then neither locks such a BO nor moves it back. Its PTEs are
updated to wherever it is now, cleared if it went to system memory, and
it doesn't get the new eviction fence, so it can move again under the
running queue.

On navi48, once the BOs of an SDMA user queue are evicted from GTT
(debugfs amdgpu_evict_gtt) the queue faults on its ring and rptr:

  amdgpu 0000:03:00.0:   in page starting at address 0x0000000100000000 from client 10
  amdgpu 0000:03:00.0: 	 Faulty UTCL2 client ID: SDMA0 (0xd)
  amdgpu 0000:03:00.0:   in page starting at address 0x0000000100101000 from client 10

Validate the BOs on the individual needs_update list like before.

(cherry picked from commit eb0d94765d4be18d41e93ad09947dd9cc06ed31a)

summary: assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one

When a full node's leaves and the new key all share the node's segment,
assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node() replaces the node with a
shortcut to a pair of new nodes.  If the node is itself the target of a
shortcut, the new shortcut is installed as that shortcut's next node,
and a shortcut leading to a shortcut is something nothing expects:
assoc_array_walk() indexes the second one as a node, and
assoc_array_apply_edit() hits the BUG_ON() in the loop that adjusts
nr_leaves_on_branch, on that same insertion.

Deletion gets a node there.  When the subtree below a shortcut shrinks
enough, assoc_array_delete() collapses it into one node below the
shortcut, and the leaves it collects can all share that node's segment.
The next key that shares it too takes this path.  Eighteen insertions
and a deletion are enough: sixteen keys that agree on bits 0-11, one
that leaves them at bit 8 and is deleted again, and one more that agrees
with the sixteen.

Have the new shortcut replace the one in front of the node as well.
assoc_array_insert_shortcut() gives it that shortcut's back pointer and
parent slot, so the caller installs it where that one was, and excises
the old shortcut along with the node, which takes a second entry in
excised_meta[].  The new shortcut's index key comes from the new key up
to the new skip level, so it covers what the old one did.

Found by a userspace test doing random insertions and deletions on keys
that share long prefixes; a targeted case builds a shortcut, deletes
down to the collapse and inserts one more key.

summary: f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack

sit_ver_bitmap_bytesize and nat_ver_bitmap_bytesize are used as memcpy
lengths into and out of sbi->ckpt, which is sized from cp_payload alone,
and nothing compares either length against that allocation.

sanity_check_ckpt() has checked these two fields since c77ec61ca0a4, which
added them after a crafted image overran build_sit_info(). That check ties
each length to a segment count; it never compares either against the
allocation, which is the half this adds.

Mounting over-reads in build_sit_info() and build_node_manager(), and the
first checkpoint writes the same lengths back through the same pointers,
so the over-read's contents reach the on-disk checkpoint. An unmount is
enough; the filesystem does not have to be used.

Bound both ends the way __bitmap_ptr() lays them out. The three branches
differ, so a single sum of the two lengths would still admit a small
overflow when cp_payload is non-zero.

summary: ksmbd: prevent session binding in compound requests
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: prevent session binding in compound requests

A failed multichannel binding can retain its target session on the work
item so that the error response can be signed. Subsequent compound
commands can then use that session together with a tree connection left
over from an earlier command.

Limit binding SESSION_SETUP requests to standalone messages during
message validation, before smb2_sess_setup() can replace work->sess.
Check both NextCommand and the current request offset to cover binding
in the first, middle and last positions of a compound. The existing
validation error path returns STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER and stops
processing the remaining commands.

This intentionally limits support for compounded binding. It is not a
protocol requirement that binding be standalone. Standalone binding and
non-binding compounds retain their existing behavior, without changing
session, tree or response encryption handling.

summary: mm/gup: fix out-of-bounds write for nr_pages == 0 in GUP-fast
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/gup: fix out-of-bounds write for nr_pages == 0 in GUP-fast

With nr_pages == 0, GUP-fast still enters its page table walk and can
write past the caller's page array. The old end <= start check caught
empty ranges, but was replaced with an overflow check.

Users such as OrangeFS can pass a zero page count derived from a
userspace-supplied length. So let's return zero for nr_pages == 0 before
starting the walk, just like GUP-slow.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

[ david: simplify description ]

summary: ksmbd: fix OOB read and cross-share confusion in ksmbd_validate_name_reconnect()
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix OOB read and cross-share confusion in ksmbd_validate_name_reconnect()

ksmbd_validate_name_reconnect() indexes
ab_pathname[share->path_sz + 1] without checking that the path is
longer than share->path_sz + 1 (d_path() fills the buffer from the
end). A durable fp is not bound to its original share, so a client
can preserve a file from a short-path share and reconnect it on a
long-path share, making strcmp() read past the PATH_MAX buffer -
with a long enough share path this oopses the kernel, and on a
mapped page it also gives a byte-equality oracle on adjacent heap
(the reconnect succeeds exactly when the out-of-bounds string
equals the requested name). A same-share variant with the durable
fp at the share root reads 1 byte past the buffer
(strlen(ab_pathname) == share->path_sz).

Check before comparing: the path must be longer than share->path_sz,
it must start with share->path, and the next character must be '/'.
The share root itself is accepted only for an empty name.

summary: Drivers: hv: vmbus: Bounds check the shared ring buffer indices
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Drivers: hv: vmbus: Bounds check the shared ring buffer indices

In a CoCo VM the host is untrusted. Since the VMBus ring buffer read and
write indices live in shared memory, the guest has to treat both as
potentially malicious.

hv_ringbuffer_write() copies into the ring at write_index with no bounds
checking, so the host can make the guest write packet data at any offset
up to 4 GiB past the start of the ring buffer. read_index matters too:
the available space derived from both indices is the only bound on how
much is copied, and an out-of-range index can make it far larger than
the ring.

The fix is to validate both indices before use and to use the validated
snapshot instead of re-accessing. For invalid indices,
hv_ringbuffer_write() logs and returns -EIO.

One re-read of write_index is left unchecked in this patch:
hv_get_ring_bufferindices() fetches it again for the prev_indices
trailer. The value is only returned to the host and is not used as an
offset or length for indexing. Since this is not a security issue, it is
addressed later in the series.

Open-coding the bytes available arithmetic keeps the fix free of
prerequisites; a later patch refactors it into a helper function.

summary: can: dev: can_dropped_invalid_skb: drop CAN XL frames on non-CAN XL devices
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

can: dev: can_dropped_invalid_skb: drop CAN XL frames on non-CAN XL devices

Sending a PF_PACKET bypasses the CAN framework logic and can directly
reach a CAN driver's xmit() function. The PF_PACKET framework only
checks that skb->len does not exceed the net_device MTU.

For a CAN device that is not CAN XL capable, anything above CANFD_MTU
(72 bytes) is therefore dropped before it reaches the driver. However,
CAN XL frames are variable length. can_is_canxl_skb() accepts lengths in
the range CANXL_HDR_SIZE + CANXL_MIN_DLEN up to CANXL_MTU, i.e. 13 to
2060 bytes.

As a result, an ETH_P_CANXL skb with a length between 13 and 72 bytes
can pass both the MTU and the can_dropped_invalid_skb() checks.

A driver that does not support CAN XL will interpret canxl_frame->flags
as a length because of the overlap with can_frame->len. And because
CANXL_XLF is set, the resulting length is between 128 and 255. For
drivers that do not check can_frame->len before copying can_frame->data,
as most drivers do, this results in a buffer overflow of up to 247
bytes.

Drop ETH_P_CANXL skbs if the device does not have the CAN_CAP_XL
capability. Keep can_is_canxl_skb() for the validation of CAN XL skbs.

summary: smb: smbdirect: release failed pending sockets of a listener
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: release failed pending sockets of a listener

A child of a listener only left the listen.pending or listen.ready
list via smbdirect_socket_accept() or when the listener was
destroyed. So every connection that failed before it was accepted
(negotiate timeout, peer disconnect, invalid negotiate request, ...)
stayed on the list and counted against the backlog until the listener
was destroyed. After about backlog (10 for ksmbd) such connections
smbdirect_listen_connect_request() rejected every new connection with
-EBUSY, so an unauthenticated peer was able to permanently stop
ksmbd from accepting SMB-Direct connections.

Now a failed child moves itself to a new listen.orphaned list at the
end of smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work(), after the disconnect was
started, and queues listen.purge_orphaned_work, which releases it
with smbdirect_socket_release(), without holding the listener's
rdma_lock_handler() lock, in the same way smbdirect_socket_destroy()
does for the remaining children. Orphaned sockets still count against
the backlog until they are released.

sc->accept.listener is now only changed under listener->listen.lock
and whoever clears it is responsible for releasing the socket:
smbdirect_socket_accept(), purge_orphaned_work or the destroy of the
listener.

In order to make that work:

- a struct smbdirect_socket that is a listener is now freed via
  kfree_rcu(), so that a child can dereference sc->accept.listener
  under rcu_read_lock(), even if the listener is released concurrently.

- smbdirect_listen_connect_request() adds nsc to the listen.pending
  list and sets nsc->accept.listener before it calls
  smbdirect_accept_connect_request(), and always returns 0 so the
  rdma_cm core keeps the connection id and nsc owns it. On a non-zero
  return it schedules nsc's teardown with
  smbdirect_socket_schedule_cleanup(), which orphans it off the
  listener so that purge_orphaned_work releases it; nsc destroys its
  own connection id with rdma_destroy_id() in that teardown. The
  teardown has to be deferred because the rdma_cm core holds nsc's
  id_priv->handler_mutex across the handler, so nsc->rdma.cm_id must
  not be destroyed synchronously from here. That same handler_mutex
  (and the listener's) also guarantees nsc can't go away under us,
  so setting the listener before the call is safe and lets a failure
  orphan nsc.

- smbdirect_accept_negotiate_recv_work() no longer moves a socket to
  the ready list if it already failed or no longer belongs to the
  listener. Every accepting socket has a listener, so if
  sc->accept.listener is already cleared, it no longer sends a
  negotiate response, as the socket is about to be released.

- smbdirect_socket_destroy() of the listener disables
  purge_orphaned_work and also releases the orphaned sockets.

summary: RDMA/uverbs: Fix DMABUF use-after-free during ufile cleanup
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

RDMA/uverbs: Fix DMABUF use-after-free during ufile cleanup

The DMABUF release can race with ufile cleanup. When the cleanup holds
hw_destroy_rwsem for write, uverbs_uobject_release() fails its trylock
and leaves the uobject on the ufile list, but the dma_buf is freed as
soon as the release returns. The cleanup then destroys the uobject and
uses the freed dma_buf:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in uverbs_dmabuf_fd_destroy_uobj+0x46/0x200
  Read of size 8 at addr ff11000109cf14b0 by task repro/435
  Call Trace:
   uverbs_dmabuf_fd_destroy_uobj+0x46/0x200
   destroy_hw_fd_uobject+0x3f/0x50
   uverbs_destroy_uobject+0xc5/0x380
   __uverbs_cleanup_ufile+0x1a8/0x260
   uverbs_destroy_ufile_hw+0x54/0x160
   ib_uverbs_close+0x34/0x110
  Allocated by task 435:
   dma_buf_export+0x1b5/0x530
   ib_uverbs_handler_UVERBS_METHOD_DMABUF_ALLOC+0x223/0x3f0
  Freed by task 436:
   kfree+0x301/0x530
   dentry_kill+0x14c/0x560
   __fput+0x23a/0x4a0

rdma_user_mmap_entry_remove() dereferences the same pointer.

Protect the stored dma_buf pointer with a mutex and clear it before
release returns. Use a shared revoke helper so uobject destruction and
mmap entry removal both skip a cleared pointer. Hold a temporary uobject
reference across uverbs_uobject_release() and the pointer update.

Use a separate mutex because uobject destruction can free the mmap entry
before release finishes. Map and unmap use attachment->dmabuf directly,
so they do not need to take the new mutex while holding the reservation
lock.

summary: mptcp: pm: kernel: use RCU to free endpoint listeners
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mptcp: pm: kernel: use RCU to free endpoint listeners

mptcp_pm_nl_create_listen_socket() starts the TCP listener directly
instead of going through mptcp_listen(). It consequently misses setting
SOCK_RCU_FREE on the parent MPTCP socket.

tcp_child_process() can invoke the listener's subflow_data_ready()
callback without holding the MPTCP parent lock or a reference to the
parent. An authenticated MP_JOIN racing with endpoint teardown can
therefore access the parent after its last reference has been dropped.
The ADD_ADDR error path can also close an already published listener.

Set SOCK_RCU_FREE before __inet_listen_sk() publishes the TCP listener,
matching mptcp_listen(). This protects the parent on every subsequent
close path, including a failed endpoint addition.

summary: mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings
details:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings

find_vma_and_prepare_anon() can end up allocating an anon_vma in VMAs that
are not CoW mappings, which is wrong.

If we have a MAP_SHARED R/O file mapped, we lack VM_SHARED (but do have
VM_MAYSHARE) and lack VM_MAYWRITE.

While uffd later rejects such mappings (uffd registration requires
VM_MAYWRITE, see comment in validate_dst_vma) find_vma_and_prepare_anon()
